title: GIAC GXPN
summary: The GIAC Exploit Researcher and Advanced Penetration Tester certification, exam code GXPN, is an advanced offensive security credential from GIAC, the certification body of the SANS Institute. It suits experienced penetration testers, exploit developers, red team operators and security researchers who already understand basic testing and now want to attack hardened systems. Passing it shows an employer that you can research a target, defeat modern memory protections, write and adapt working proof of concept code, break weak cryptography in use, and reach well protected internal systems. The exam is proctored and combines multiple choice questions with performance based items that require real work in a live environment, and GIAC exams allow a printed index that you build yourself. A pass is valid for several years and is renewed through continuing education credits. It leads to roles such as senior penetration tester, exploit developer, red team lead or vulnerability researcher. This certification assumes strong prior knowledge, and GIAC revises its outline from time to time, so confirm the current version before you book. This is an independent study guide and it is not approved or sponsored by GIAC or SANS.

beginner.definition: This is an advanced certification from GIAC about finding and using serious software weaknesses. An exploit is a small piece of work that uses a bug to make a program behave in a way its author did not intend. The exam is meant for people who already test systems and now want deeper skills. It is one of the harder offensive security certifications to pass.
beginner.whyItMatters: Real attackers do not stop at a simple bug, and defenders must understand advanced techniques to stop them. This certificate proves you can go beyond running other people tools and build your own understanding. It supports senior tester, researcher and red team roles, which carry more responsibility and higher pay. It also strengthens your ability to explain risk to engineers who write the code. Expect to invest serious study time before you sit the exam.
howItWorks: Make sure your basics are solid first, because this exam assumes network and host testing skills.
Build a lab with older and newer systems so you can watch protections change behaviour.
Study memory layout and the common defences one by one, such as non executable memory.
Practise writing small scripts and proof of concept code instead of only using ready tools.
Learn how weak keys, poor randomness and bad protocol design can be broken.
Build a printed index and take the official practice test to judge your readiness honestly.
beginner.example: Picture an internal server that a client believes is safe because it is patched. Your first attempt fails, because the operating system now randomises where code sits in memory. Instead of giving up, you read the program carefully, find a way to leak an address, and use that leak to write a working proof. The exam rewards that patient method. It asks how you would approach a protected target and why one technique works where another does not, not simply which tool name to type.
takeaways: This is an advanced exam, so build your foundations before you attempt it.
You must practise writing your own code, because ready made tools are not enough.
Deep understanding of one technique beats shallow knowledge of many tools.

objectives: Explain how memory is organised and how modern protections change an attack.
Analyse network protocols and services for exploitable behaviour.
Identify and exploit weaknesses in cryptographic implementations and keys.
Develop and adapt working proof of concept code against a target.
Bypass host protections and escalate privileges on a hardened system.
Use reverse engineering and fuzzing to find new software flaws.

chapters.title: Network attacks and password attacks
objectives: Analyse captured traffic to find weaknesses in a protocol implementation.
Attack authentication protocols used on internal networks.
Explain how password storage and cracking methods differ in speed and cost.
Use tunnelling and traffic manipulation techniques during an assessment.
Assess the business impact of a successful network level attack.

chapters.title: Cryptographic attacks and weaknesses
objectives: Identify weak keys, poor randomness and unsafe modes of operation.
Attack a system that reuses values it should never reuse.
Explain how padding and implementation errors break otherwise strong algorithms.
Assess certificate handling and trust decisions for exploitable mistakes.
Recommend the correction that removes the weakness, not just the symptom.

chapters.title: Host exploitation and privilege escalation
objectives: Describe how a program uses memory and where unsafe input can change it.
Explain how address randomisation, data execution prevention and canaries work.
Build a working exploit that defeats the protections in place on a target.
Bypass sandboxes, filters and application level restrictions.
Escalate privileges to the highest level available on a compromised host.

chapters.title: Reverse engineering, fuzzing and research
objectives: Read compiled code with a disassembler and explain what a routine does.
Debug a running program to observe how it handles input.
Fuzz a target to find crashes that may be exploitable.
Judge whether a crash can be turned into reliable code execution.
Write up a new finding so another researcher can reproduce it.
